text:
10:47 RE gpu utilization issue: if I were a gamedev, I would want the GPU utilization to be below 100% all the time, everytime. 95-99% is a good ballpark. (Also, the 4060 dipped to lower util% during your explanation) Keeping GPU utilization pinned at 100% causes CPU drawcall backpressure, leading to increased input latency. The CPU did all the calculations for input registration and advancing the game state simulation. Along with a few thousand draw calls, this info gets put into a render queue for the GPU. If the GPU is too slow to keep the queue empty, then those prepared draw calls and the player input data "inside" of those get "stale". Every milisecond that the render queue is populated, is an additional ms of input latency. You don't want 100% GPU utilization, ever. We want the current frame being calculated in the GPU to be with the most recent input data available. 
However, for optimal input latency, we need to control the GPU util% by applying a framerate limit on the CPU frame preparation side of the equation. (In-engine framerate limiter, or rivatuner statistics server on windows. FPS limiters in the GPU driver do not help this issue)
This is the mechanical basis on which Nvidia Reflex works. Reflex is just a dynamic framerate limiter, where the framerate limit dynamically decreases to always keep GPU util at 99% or lower. But games can also implement this themselves, and have been for a decade in the case of CS2/CSGO (which is also why nvidia reflex does nothing in that game, its just to keep uninformed gamers happy) At least, I suspect as much, since I was never able to get CSGO to run at 100% GPU util on any of the systems I owned in the last 10 years.

If you need any sources to back my bullshit up, watch Battlenonsense video titled "NVIDIA Reflex Low Latency - How It Works & Why You Want To Use It". That guy most likely gave nvidia the idea for reflex way back in the day during his fps input latency testing.

text:
Yeah it's great that intel (and AMD) are putting out reasonably priced low-mid range cards. Buuuut....you're trying to sell the performance by comparing it against cards that came out 2-4 years ago.

A 15% performance lead over a 4 year old gpu, isn't really exciting, nor is it matching(ish) the performance of a bottom of the barrel 2 year old card...especially when you can snag that 6600xt for $80-$100 used. 

Had they actually managed to launch the first gen cards when they intended, 2020....things would probably be a bit different. But they didn't. 

Also, GPU's have not been "terrible" Raw, brute force performance simply isn't the focus anymore. We already have cards that will do 200 FPS at 4k when it comes to pure raster.....Esports titles are outputting 600+fps at 1080p, and 300+ at 4k. Are we complaining because the new cards aren't going to push those frame rates over 1000fps? 

Gamers running 4k is less than 5%, 1440p accounts for about 20, 1080p accounts for 55%....and the remainder are running BELOW 1080p. Ray/path tracing is the future....and it's insanely computationally expensive. When i first started in CAD/computer animation/digital art 28 years ago, at 11 years old....bryce 3d had path tracing built into it's render engine. It took 37.5 hours, to render an omni-directional light source, in a black void, at 1024x768. That's 9.4%  the pixel density of 4k. Without ray/path tracing? 6 minutes. 

Today, 1 frame of a pixar movie takes 50 hours to render...and they're making use of supercomputing server farms.

That's the overhead.

The 1080 ti, which launched in 2017, had 3584 cuda cores, and 11.8  billion transistors
The 5090 will clock in at 21,760 cuda cores, and 92.2 billion transistors. And still....it struggles with having enough raw performance to maintain playable frame rates with path tracing....are we  going to get to the point where that's no longer a problem? Maybe! But until that time arrives....to get the increase to visual fidelity, requires changing the metrics by which we judge performance.

text:
Hey, great video!
I have a few questions:
Do you maybe have the possibility to add a second B580 to your rig?
Of course, technologies like SLI and Crossfire are no longer a thing, but it seems like you could offload the heavy calculations of the Lossless Scaler to a second GPU. The idea is that the main GPU used for rendering wouldn't be affected by the extra calculations.
However, it doesn’t seem to work with many GPU combinations, possibly because of the PCIe 16x split into 2x 8x, which might cause a bottleneck due to the heavy communication between the GPUs. Or maybe it's because the tested GPUs had different bandwidths and needed to adapt first – I’m not entirely sure. It would be interesting to see a test with similar GPUs to eliminate most of these variables.

By the way, some users have reported significant performance improvements with their mobile GPUs by utilizing the iGPU for the Lossless Scaler.

On the settings side, I’d say it’s crucial to get close to 60 FPS as a baseline (this can be monitored with RivaTuner). From there, you can scale up to your screen’s limit for a smoother experience.
The resolution scale can be lowered – it makes the motion a bit blurrier but is barely noticeable unless you reduce it too much. I’d say scaling it down to 80% works great. I wouldn’t upscale unless absolutely necessary.

I’m not using this setup primarily for gaming. Instead, I use it to cut the energy consumption of my RTX 3080 in half, without any noticeable quality differences.
